title: Canon, Manuscripts and Translation
bigQuestion: How did the Bible come to have the books, the wording and the words it has in the copy on your desk?

story.title: Pages in a Basket
story.kicker: In a monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai, a German scholar found leaves of a Greek Bible copied in the fourth century.
paragraphs: In May 1844 a young scholar named Constantin von Tischendorf arrived at the Monastery of Saint Catherine, at the foot of the mountain tradition calls Sinai. He was hunting for old manuscripts. In a hall of the monastery, by his own account, he saw a basket holding old parchment leaves. He said a monk told him two such baskets had already been burned. Tischendorf recognized the large, clear Greek letters at once as very old. He was allowed to take forty-three leaves back to Europe.

The monastery has always disputed the basket story, and historians treat Tischendorf's account with caution. What is not in doubt is what the leaves were. They came from a codex, a bound book rather than a scroll, written in Greek in the middle of the fourth century, c. 330–360 CE. It held the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, and a complete New Testament, plus two early Christian writings, the Epistle of Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas. Scholars named it Codex Sinaiticus.

Tischendorf returned in 1853 and 1859. On the last visit a monk showed him the rest of the codex, and it eventually went to the Russian tsar, whose ambassador sponsored the trip. In 1933 the Soviet government sold most of it to the British Museum for one hundred thousand pounds. Today its leaves are divided between London, Leipzig, Saint Petersburg and the monastery itself, which found more leaves in 1975. Since 2009 the whole codex has been available online.

Why did this matter so much? Sinaiticus is one of the two oldest nearly complete Bibles in the world. Its text differs in thousands of small ways from the later manuscripts behind the King James Bible. It ends the gospel of Mark at 16:8, without the twelve verses printed in most Bibles. Reading it forced scholars to ask hard questions. Which books belong? Which wording is oldest? And once you know, how do you put it into English? Those three questions are this chapter.
story.think: A fourth-century Bible includes two books no modern Bible prints and ends Mark early. What would you want to know before deciding what to do with that information?

lessons.title: The Hebrew Canon
lessons.mainIdea: The Jewish canon, the Tanakh, has three parts, and its contents settled over centuries rather than at a single meeting.
reading: The word *canon* comes from a Greek word for a measuring rod. In the study of the Bible it means the list of books a community counts as scripture. Jewish tradition calls its Bible the Tanakh, from the initials of its three parts: Torah (teaching, the five books of Moses), Nevi'im (prophets) and Ketuvim (writings). Counted the Jewish way, it holds twenty-four books; the same texts counted the Protestant way make thirty-nine, because Samuel, Kings, Chronicles and the twelve minor prophets are split.

The three parts seem to have gained authority in stages. The Torah was read publicly by the time of Ezra, in the fifth century BCE (Nehemiah 8). The prologue to the book of Sirach, written c. 132 BCE, already speaks of the law, the prophets and the other books. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing c. 95 CE, said his people had twenty-two books they held sacred (Against Apion 1.8). The edges of the Writings, books such as Esther, Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs, were still discussed by rabbis in the second century CE (Mishnah, Yadayim 3:5).

Older textbooks said the Jewish canon was fixed at a council in Yavneh, or Jamnia, c. 90 CE. Most scholars now doubt that any such formal council took place; the rabbis at Yavneh discussed some books, but the canon grew by use over time. That is a good example of how a tidy story gets corrected. It also shows that a canon is not usually made by a single vote. Communities read certain books, copied them, taught from them, and over generations the list hardened.

words.d: the list of books a community counts as scripture; from a Greek word for a measuring rod
the Jewish Bible, named from the initials of Torah, Nevi'im (prophets) and Ketuvim (writings)
the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh, including Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Esther and Daniel
a town, also called Jamnia, where rabbis gathered after 70 CE; once wrongly said to have fixed the canon by council

lessons.title: The Septuagint and the Apocrypha
lessons.mainIdea: The Greek Septuagint included books not in the Hebrew canon, and Jewish, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles differ over them to this day.
reading: In the third century BCE the Jews of Alexandria, in Egypt, spoke Greek. Tradition told in the Letter of Aristeas says that seventy-two scholars translated the Torah into Greek for the king's library, and the translation was named the *Septuagint*, from the Latin for seventy. Historians accept that the Torah was translated in Alexandria c. 250 BCE and the rest over the following two centuries; the story of the seventy-two is a legend that grew. The Septuagint became the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and then of the early church. Most Old Testament quotations in the New Testament follow its wording.

Greek manuscripts of the Septuagint carried books and passages that the Hebrew canon does not: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Baruch, 1 and 2 Maccabees, and additions to Esther and Daniel. Protestants call these the *Apocrypha*, hidden things; Catholics call them deuterocanonical, a second canon, and count them as scripture. Orthodox churches include those and a few more. Jewish tradition does not include them, though Hanukkah recalls events told in 1 Maccabees. Jerome doubted their standing; the Council of Trent (1546) affirmed it for Catholics.

The result is that the number of books in a Bible depends on whose Bible it is. Protestant Bibles have 66; Catholic Bibles 73; Greek Orthodox Bibles a few more; the Ethiopian Orthodox canon is larger still. The King James Bible of 1611 printed the Apocrypha between the Testaments, and most editions dropped it in the nineteenth century. When a public-school class reads the Bible, then, the first question is which one, and a fair answer names all of them.

words.d: the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible begun in Alexandria c. 250 BCE; named from the Latin for seventy
the books in Greek and Latin Bibles but not the Hebrew canon; Protestants use this name, Catholics say deuterocanonical
the Catholic term for books such as Tobit, Judith and 1–2 Maccabees, a second canon counted as scripture

look.title: How Many Books?
look.cite: Standard canon lists; Ethiopian and Orthodox totals vary by how books are counted

check.q: What do Catholics call the books Protestants call the Apocrypha?
check.why: Catholics count these books as a second canon and call them deuterocanonical.

lessons.title: Marcion, the Muratorian Fragment and Athanasius
lessons.mainIdea: The New Testament canon took shape between about 140 and 367 CE, through a rejected proposal, early lists and a bishop's letter.
reading: The first known person to propose a fixed Christian scripture was Marcion, a wealthy shipowner who taught in Rome c. 144 CE. He held that the God of the Hebrew Bible was a different, lesser being from the Father of Jesus. So his scripture had no Old Testament at all: only an edited gospel of Luke and ten letters of Paul. The church in Rome expelled him. Many historians think Marcion's list pushed other Christians to say more clearly which books they did accept, though the extent of his influence is debated.

The *Muratorian fragment* is a damaged Latin list discovered in a Milan library and published by Ludovico Muratori in 1740. Most scholars date the original to the late second century, though some argue for the fourth. It names four gospels, Acts, thirteen letters of Paul, Jude, two letters of John, the Wisdom of Solomon and Revelation, and it admits the Apocalypse of Peter with some hesitation. It leaves out Hebrews, James and the letters of Peter. The list shows a canon largely, but not fully, agreed by then.

The earliest surviving list that names exactly the twenty-seven books of today's New Testament, and no others, is the Easter letter of *Athanasius*, bishop of Alexandria, in 367 CE. He called them the springs of salvation and said no one should add to them or take from them. Councils at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) confirmed similar lists in the West. No emperor decided the matter, and the Council of Nicaea in 325 did not discuss the canon, despite a popular modern legend. The list emerged from use, argument and, at last, agreement.

words.d: a teacher in Rome c. 144 CE who rejected the Hebrew Bible and kept an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul; expelled by the church
a damaged Latin list of New Testament books, published in 1740 and usually dated to the late second century
bishop of Alexandria whose Easter letter of 367 CE is the earliest list naming exactly the 27 New Testament books

lessons.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
lessons.mainIdea: Scrolls found near the Dead Sea from 1947 pushed the oldest known Hebrew Bible manuscripts back by about a thousand years.
reading: Before 1947 the oldest complete Hebrew Bible manuscript was the Leningrad Codex, copied in 1008 CE, and the slightly older Aleppo Codex, c. 930 CE, now missing parts. These were the work of the *Masoretes*, Jewish scribes who added vowel marks and notes to fix the text between roughly 600 and 1000 CE. Their text, the Masoretic Text, is the Hebrew Bible behind almost every Jewish and Christian translation. But a thousand years separated it from the last books of the Bible, and no one knew how much had changed.

In 1947 Bedouin shepherds found jars holding scrolls in a cave near Qumran, by the northwest shore of the Dead Sea. Over the next decade eleven caves yielded some nine hundred manuscripts, most in fragments, written in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek and dated by script and by radiocarbon to c. 250 BCE to 68 CE. The *Dead Sea Scrolls* include copies of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther, along with community rules, hymns and commentaries. Many scholars connect them to a Jewish group living at Qumran, often identified with the Essenes; that identification is debated.

The star find is the Great Isaiah Scroll, a complete copy of Isaiah about 24 feet long, dated c. 125 BCE. Compared with the Leningrad Codex, copied more than eleven centuries later, its text is remarkably close, with mostly small differences in spelling and wording. Other scrolls, however, show that more than one form of some books circulated: a shorter Jeremiah like the Septuagint's, a Samuel with readings the Greek shares. The scrolls proved both how carefully scribes copied and that the text was not yet fixed to a single form.

words.d: Jewish scribes, c. 600–1000 CE, who added vowel marks and notes to fix the Hebrew text; their text is the Masoretic Text
about nine hundred manuscripts found from 1947 in caves near Qumran, dated c. 250 BCE–68 CE
the site near the northwest shore of the Dead Sea where the scrolls were found
a complete copy of Isaiah from Qumran, c. 125 BCE, the best-preserved of the scrolls

lessons.title: Codices and Papyri
lessons.mainIdea: The New Testament survives in thousands of Greek manuscripts, from tiny second-century papyrus scraps to complete fourth-century codices.
reading: No original manuscript of any biblical book survives. What survives are copies, and for the New Testament there are a great many: about 5,800 Greek manuscripts, from scraps to complete Bibles, plus thousands in Latin, Syriac, Coptic and other languages. The earliest are written on *papyrus*, a paper made from a Nile reed. The oldest generally accepted piece is P52, a fragment of John 18 the size of a credit card, kept in Manchester, England, and usually dated c. 125–175 CE. P46, a codex of Paul's letters, dates from c. 200.

The great fourth-century codices are written on parchment, prepared animal skin, in capital letters with no spaces between words, a style called uncial. *Codex Vaticanus*, in the Vatican Library since at least 1475, and *Codex Sinaiticus*, the manuscript from the opening story, both date to c. 325–360 CE. Codex Alexandrinus, in the British Library, is from the fifth century. These three, with the papyri, are the main witnesses scholars use to reconstruct the earliest recoverable text of the New Testament.

The shift from scroll to *codex* mattered. A scroll holds one long book; a codex can hold a whole library between two covers. Christians adopted the codex early and almost completely, while Jewish communities kept the scroll for synagogue reading, as they do today. Some historians think the codex made it possible to think of the many books as one Bible. A canon list and a bound book reinforce each other: once all the books sit inside a single cover, the question of which books belong has a physical answer.

words.d: writing material made from a Nile reed; the earliest New Testament manuscripts are papyrus fragments
a bound book with pages, as opposed to a scroll; Christians adopted it early
a Greek Bible of the fourth century kept in the Vatican Library, one of the two oldest nearly complete Bibles
a Greek Bible of the fourth century found at Saint Catherine's Monastery, now mostly in the British Library

lessons.title: Textual Criticism and the Ending of Mark
lessons.mainIdea: Textual critics compare manuscripts to recover the earliest wording; the last twelve verses of Mark are the best-known case where they differ.
reading: Copyists made mistakes: skipped lines, doubled words, misheard dictation. Sometimes they also made changes on purpose, smoothing grammar or adding a familiar phrase from another gospel. So manuscripts differ, and a place where they differ is called a *variant*. Scholars count hundreds of thousands of variants across the Greek New Testament manuscripts, most of them spelling and word order that change no meaning. *Textual criticism* is the discipline of comparing the copies to decide which reading is most likely original.

Its rules are simple to state. Prefer the reading in the oldest and best manuscripts. Prefer the harder reading, since scribes smoothed rather than roughened. Prefer the reading that best explains how the others arose. The most famous case is the *ending of Mark*. In Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, Mark ends at 16:8 with the women fleeing the tomb, afraid, and telling no one. Most later manuscripts add twelve verses, 16:9–20, with appearances of the risen Jesus, snake handling and a command to preach. A few have a different short ending.

Eusebius in the fourth century and Jerome around 400 both noted that most Greek copies they knew lacked the longer ending. Its vocabulary differs from the rest of Mark. Most scholars conclude that 16:9–20 was added in the second century, perhaps because an ending at afraid seemed unbearable. Modern translations print the verses with a bracket or note. The King James Bible prints them without comment, because the manuscripts its translators used included them. Christians differ on the verses' authority; nothing central to Christian teaching rests on them alone. Two other well-known variants are the story of the woman taken in adultery (John 7:53–8:11) and the Trinitarian phrase in 1 John 5:7, which is absent from all early Greek manuscripts.

words.d: a place where manuscripts of the same text differ in wording
the discipline of comparing manuscripts to decide which reading is most likely the earliest
Mark 16:9–20, twelve verses absent from the oldest manuscripts, which end at 16:8

check.why: A copyist is more likely to make a rough reading smooth than the reverse, so the harder reading is more likely original.

check.why: Jerome, c. 400, and before him Eusebius, remarked that the verses were missing from most Greek manuscripts.

lessons.title: Jerome and the Vulgate
lessons.mainIdea: Jerome's Latin Bible, made c. 382–405 from Hebrew and Greek, became the Bible of Western Europe for a thousand years.
reading: By the fourth century most Christians in the western Roman Empire spoke Latin, and Latin translations of the Bible had multiplied, of uneven quality. In 382 Pope Damasus asked a scholar named *Jerome* to revise the Latin gospels against the Greek. Jerome went further. Settling in Bethlehem, he learned Hebrew from Jewish teachers and translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew rather than from the Septuagint, finishing c. 405. He called this the Hebrew truth, and it caused controversy, since the Septuagint had been the church's Old Testament.

Jerome's version came to be called the *Vulgate*, from a Latin word meaning common or widely used. It was not accepted overnight. Augustine worried that congregations would be upset by unfamiliar wording; he told Jerome of a church in North Africa that rioted when the plant in Jonah 4 was read as ivy instead of gourd. Over the following centuries the Vulgate won out. It was the Bible Wycliffe translated from, the first book Gutenberg printed, c. 1455, and the Bible the Council of Trent declared authentic for Catholic use in 1546.

Jerome also gave later translators their hardest questions. He judged that the books found only in Greek, the Apocrypha, should be read for edification but not used to establish doctrine, a view Protestants later took up. And in Isaiah 7:14 he rendered the Hebrew word almah with the Latin virgo, virgin, following the Septuagint's Greek, a choice that a later lesson returns to. Every translation decides, and the Vulgate's decisions shaped Western Christianity for a millennium.

words.d: the scholar (c. 347–420) who translated the Bible into Latin from Hebrew and Greek, working mostly in Bethlehem
Jerome's Latin Bible, from a word meaning common; the Bible of Western Europe for a thousand years
Jerome's phrase for translating the Old Testament from the Hebrew rather than from the Greek Septuagint

Jerome replied that he had followed the Hebrew as best he could.
look.prompt: Whose side would you take, the bishop who kept the familiar reading or Jerome who followed the Hebrew? What does the episode show about why new translations cause trouble?

check.q: What does the name Vulgate mean?
check.why: Vulgate comes from the Latin vulgata, the common edition.

check.q: Which council declared the Vulgate authentic for Catholic use?
check.why: The Council of Trent in 1546 declared the Vulgate the authentic Latin text; Nicaea did not discuss the Bible's text or canon.

lessons.title: Wycliffe and Tyndale
lessons.mainIdea: Putting the Bible into English was dangerous: Wycliffe's followers were persecuted, and Tyndale, whose words fill the King James Bible, was executed in 1536.
reading: The first complete English Bible is linked to *John Wycliffe*, an Oxford scholar who held that scripture, not the church, was the final authority. His followers produced it from the Vulgate c. 1382–1395; Wycliffe himself died in 1384, and how much he translated is unknown. The church condemned the movement, called Lollards. In 1408 English bishops forbade any new translation without approval, and in 1428 Wycliffe's bones were dug up and burned. About 250 manuscripts of the Wycliffe Bible survive, more than of any other medieval English text.

*William Tyndale* changed everything by using two new tools: the printing press and the Greek New Testament that Erasmus published in 1516. Refused permission in England, he fled to the continent and printed his English New Testament in Worms in 1526. Copies were smuggled into England in bales of cloth and burned by the bishop of London. Tyndale went on to translate the Pentateuch and other books from Hebrew. Betrayed in Antwerp, he was strangled and burned near Brussels in 1536. His reported last words were a prayer that the king of England's eyes be opened.

Tyndale's English survives on a scale most readers never notice. Phrases such as let there be light, the powers that be, my brother's keeper and the salt of the earth are his. He coined the words Passover and scapegoat. Scholars estimate that most of the King James New Testament repeats his wording. Within a year of his death, an English Bible with royal license, largely Tyndale's work, was legally on sale. Miles Coverdale had printed the first complete English Bible in 1535, filling in Tyndale's unfinished Old Testament from Latin and German.

words.d: an Oxford scholar (d. 1384) whose followers made the first complete English Bible, from the Vulgate
the translator (c. 1494–1536) who printed the first English New Testament from Greek, executed in 1536
the followers of Wycliffe, persecuted for reading and teaching the Bible in English
the Dutch scholar who published the first printed Greek New Testament in 1516, the base for Tyndale and Luther

check.why: Wycliffe's followers worked from the Latin Vulgate; Greek and Hebrew texts were not yet available in England.

check.q: Which two tools made Tyndale's translation possible?

lessons.title: The King James Bible of 1611
lessons.mainIdea: Commissioned in 1604 and published in 1611, the King James Bible was a committee revision that became the most influential book in English.
reading: In 1604 the new king of England, James I, called a conference at Hampton Court to hear the complaints of Puritan clergy. One request was a new translation. James agreed, partly because he disliked the notes in the popular Geneva Bible of 1560, which questioned the rights of kings. About forty-seven scholars in six companies, at Oxford, Cambridge and Westminster, divided the books between them. Their instructions told them to revise the Bishops' Bible of 1568, keep old church words such as church rather than congregation, and add no doctrinal notes.

The *King James Version* appeared in 1611. It was not a fresh translation but a careful revision, checked against Hebrew and Greek, and it kept most of Tyndale's New Testament wording. Its Greek base was the printed text descended from Erasmus, later called the Textus Receptus, which rests on late medieval manuscripts. It printed the Apocrypha between the Testaments. Early printings had errors; a 1631 edition left the word not out of the seventh commandment and was nicknamed the Wicked Bible.

The King James Bible was slow to displace the Geneva Bible, but by the eighteenth century it was the Bible of the English-speaking world, carried to America and read by Lincoln, Douglass and King. Its rhythms shaped English prose. Because it was published before the fourth-century codices were studied and before the papyri were found, its text differs in many places from what scholars now judge oldest. That is not a fault of the translators, who used what they had; it is the reason the next lesson exists.

words.d: the English Bible of 1611, made by six companies of scholars at the king's command; also called the Authorized Version
the English Bible of 1560, with study notes, popular with Puritans and the Bible of Shakespeare's England
the printed Greek text descended from Erasmus's 1516 edition, on which the King James New Testament rests
the 1604 meeting at which King James agreed to a new translation of the Bible

check.q: What was the King James Bible's relationship to earlier English Bibles?

lessons.title: One Verse, Five Translations
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1881 new translations have used older manuscripts and modern English; comparing one verse across versions shows every choice a translator makes.
reading: The Revised Version of 1881–1885 was the first major English Bible to use the fourth-century codices. Its American cousin, the American Standard Version of 1901, rendered God's name as Jehovah. The Revised Standard Version of 1952 caused a storm by translating Isaiah 7:14 with young woman rather than virgin; a few pastors burned copies. Since then translations have multiplied: the Jewish Publication Society's Tanakh (1985), the New International Version (1978), the New Revised Standard Version (1989), the English Standard Version (2001) and many more. Estimates vary, but the full Bible now exists in over 700 languages.

Translators choose a place on a line. At one end is *formal equivalence*, keeping the words and word order of the original as far as English allows; the King James, ASV and ESV lean this way. At the other is *dynamic equivalence*, giving the meaning in natural English; the NIV leans this way, and the Good News Bible further. Beyond the line are paraphrases such as The Message (2002), which restate freely. None is simply right. A formal version shows the shape of the Hebrew; a dynamic version reads more easily; a paraphrase may say what the original never did.

Set the first line of Psalm 23 side by side. Wycliffe, c. 1395, from the Latin: The Lord governeth me, and nothing shall fail to me. Coverdale, 1535: The Lord is my shepherd, I can want nothing. King James, 1611: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. American Standard, 1901: Jehovah is my shepherd; I shall not want. World English Bible: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. The Latin had lost the shepherd, which Coverdale restored from Hebrew; the divine name is handled four ways; and want has drifted in meaning, so newer versions say lack. One line, five decisions, none of them innocent.

translating meaning for meaning in natural English; the approach of the New International Version

look.text: Wycliffe (c. 1395, from Latin): The Lord governeth me, and nothing shall fail to me. Coverdale (1535): The Lord is my shepherd, I can want nothing. King James (1611): The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. American Standard (1901): Jehovah is my shepherd; I shall not want. World English Bible: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. look.prompt: List every difference. For each, say whether it comes from the source text used, from the translator's choice about God's name, or from changes in English itself.

check.q: Which translation first made major use of the fourth-century codices?
check.why: The Revised Version was the first major English Bible to draw on Sinaiticus and Vaticanus.

check.q: What is formal equivalence?
choices: Keeping the original's words and order as far as English allows
check.why: Formal equivalence stays close to the source's wording; dynamic equivalence gives meaning in natural English.

check.q: Why did Coverdale's Psalm 23 have a shepherd when Wycliffe's did not?
choices: Coverdale worked from the Hebrew tradition, Wycliffe from the Latin
check.why: The Vulgate's Latin had the Lord governs me; the Hebrew has shepherd, which Coverdale, following Hebrew-based sources, restored.

lessons.title: Who Decides What a Word Means
lessons.mainIdea: Some of the sharpest disputes between traditions rest on single words, and a fair reader can explain each choice without declaring a winner.
reading: Isaiah 7:14 is the clearest case. The Hebrew word is *almah*, a young woman of marriageable age. The Septuagint translated it with the Greek parthenos, which usually means virgin, and the gospel of Matthew quotes the Greek as fulfilled in the birth of Jesus (Matthew 1:23). Jerome's Latin followed the Greek. So the King James reads a virgin shall conceive, while the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation reads the young woman shall conceive. Christians read the verse as prophecy of Jesus; Jewish readers read it as a sign to King Ahaz about a child born in his own day. Both readings rest on a real feature of the text; neither can be settled by a dictionary alone.

Other words carry similar weight. The Hebrew hesed, in the King James mercy or lovingkindness, in newer versions steadfast love or faithfulness. The Greek word Paul uses for justify, which Augustine's Latin read as make righteous and Luther read as declare righteous. Faith of Christ or faith in Christ in Romans 3:22. In each case the original word is wider than any single English word, and a translator must pick. Some versions print alternatives in a footnote; the American Standard Version put the maiden in the margin at Isaiah 7:14. Footnotes are where translators admit they had to choose.

So who decides? In practice, committees do, and their choices reflect their communities. A translation made for a church will lean toward that church's readings; a translation made for scholars will note every alternative; a Jewish translation will not read the Prophets through the New Testament. That is not dishonesty. It is what it means to translate a text that several communities hold sacred. The skill this unit has built is to see the choice, name the reasons on each side, and say which tradition each reading belongs to.

look.title: Isaiah 7:14, Two Readings
look.text: King James Version (1611): Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. Jewish Publication Society (1917): behold, the young woman shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. The Hebrew word is almah; the Septuagint's Greek is parthenos; the Hebrew has the definite article.
look.prompt: Explain how each translation is faithful to something in the textual history. Then describe how a Christian and a Jewish reader each understand the sign, without saying which is right.

check.q: What does the Hebrew word almah mean?
choices: A young woman of marriageable age
check.why: Almah means a young woman; the Septuagint's Greek parthenos, usually virgin, is where the King James rendering comes from.

check.q: Which translation reads the young woman at Isaiah 7:14?
check.why: The 1917 JPS translation follows the Hebrew almah; the Vulgate, Septuagint and King James have virgin.

check.q: What is the fairest way to present Isaiah 7:14 in a public-school class?
choices: Explain both readings and which tradition each belongs to
Declare the King James reading correct
check.why: The course describes what the text says and how each tradition reads it, without asserting or denying either reading.

review.q: How many books does the Tanakh contain, counted the Jewish way?
review.why: The Tanakh has 24 books; the same texts make 39 in the Protestant count because several books are split.

review.q: Which fourth-century document is the earliest list naming exactly today's 27 New Testament books?
review.why: Athanasius's letter lists the 27 books; the Muratorian fragment omits several, and Nicaea did not address the canon.

review.q: Which discovery pushed the oldest Hebrew Bible manuscripts back by about a thousand years?
review.why: Before 1947 the oldest complete Hebrew manuscripts were c. 930–1008 CE; the scrolls date from c. 250 BCE–68 CE.

review.q: Where does Mark end in the oldest complete Greek manuscripts?
review.why: Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus end Mark at 16:8; the longer ending is found in most later manuscripts.

review.q: What did Jerome mean by the Hebrew truth?
choices: The Old Testament should be translated from Hebrew, not Greek
Latin was the language of scripture
review.why: Jerome translated the Old Testament from Hebrew rather than from the Septuagint, calling the Hebrew the truth.

review.q: What happened to William Tyndale in 1536?
choices: He completed the King James Bible
review.why: Tyndale was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde, near Brussels, in 1536; the King James Bible came 75 years later.

review.q: What was the King James translators' Greek base for the New Testament?
choices: The printed text descended from Erasmus, later called the Textus Receptus
review.why: The translators used printed Greek texts from Erasmus's line; Sinaiticus was not found until 1844.

review.q: Why do the King James Bible and the 1917 JPS translation differ at Isaiah 7:14?
choices: The King James follows the Septuagint's parthenos; the JPS follows the Hebrew almah
The JPS used a different chapter
The King James translators knew no Hebrew
review.why: Virgin comes through the Greek and Latin tradition; young woman renders the Hebrew almah directly.
